title: Running the project environment
text:
There are two ways to make sure a command uses your project’s Python and packages, rather than whatever your system’s global python happens to resolve to. uv makes the first one the default and, for most day-to-day work, the only one you need.

Recommended: uv run
With a uv project you normally do not need to activate anything. Prefix the command you want with uv run:
Run Python interactively:
uv run python
Run a script:
uv run analysis.py
Run JupyterLab:
uv run jupyter lab
Before running your command, uv first checks that uv.lock is still consistent with pyproject.toml, and that .venv/ is in sync with uv.lock — updating either automatically if not. This is a small but important reproducibility guarantee: uv run does not just use the project’s environment, it actively verifies it is the environment the project files currently describe, every time.
To exit the interactive Python prompt:
exit()
To stop JupyterLab, return to the terminal it is running in and press Ctrl+C (you may need to confirm the shutdown).


Optional: manually activating the virtual environment
Many Python tutorials that predate uv, or that use lower-level tools directly, describe activating a virtual environment instead. It is worth being able to recognise this pattern even if you do not use it day to day:

Windows PowerShellWindows Command PromptmacOS / Linux


.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1


.venv\Scripts\activate.bat


source .venv/bin/activate



After activation, your shell’s PATH has been modified so that plain commands, without the uv run prefix, refer to this environment:
python --version
To leave the activated environment:
deactivate






Tip



If PowerShell blocks an activation script due to its execution policy, you can simply use uv run ... instead — activation is a convenience, not a requirement, for normal uv project workflows.




Why does this distinction matter?
Activation changes your shell’s state for as long as that terminal session lasts, which is easy to forget about — a command run in a different terminal tab, or an hour later after you have moved on to another task, may silently use the wrong environment. uv run instead makes the environment an explicit, visible part of every single command, which is a better default for reproducibility: anyone reading a script or a README that uses uv run can see, from that command alone, which environment it is meant to run in.

title: Install uv
text:
uv is installed once per computer (not once per project), and then used everywhere. Choose the instructions for your operating system below.

WindowsmacOSLinux


Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and run:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
An alternative, if you have WinGet available, is:
winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e


Open Terminal and run:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
If you use Homebrew, another option is:
brew install uv


Open a terminal and run:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh



Close and reopen your terminal if the installer asks you to (this refreshes your shell’s PATH so it can find the new command), then check the install worked:
uv --version
uv 0.9.6
You should see a version number — the exact numbers will differ depending on when you install it, which is fine.






Warning



Only run installation commands from sources you trust. The commands above are taken from the official uv installation documentation; prefer fetching them from that page directly if you are ever unsure whether a copy you have seen elsewhere has been altered.



What did that actually install?
At this point, no Python interpreter has been installed yet — only uv itself, a single small executable. This is deliberate: uv is the tool that will go on to fetch, manage, and run Python interpreters on your behalf, in the next step.

title: Why does this matter for research?
What is a package manager?
Use uv to install Python
text:
With uv itself installed, we can now ask it to install a Python interpreter. Unlike the operating-system-provided Python you may already have (or the installers from python.org), uv-managed interpreters are downloaded into a location uv controls, are trivial to install side by side in multiple versions, and can be reproduced identically on another machine.
For this session we will use Python 3.13 as a concrete, current example. A research group, course, or funding body may reasonably standardise on a different supported version — the workflow is the same regardless of which one you pick.
Install it with:
uv python install 3.13
Installed Python 3.13.7 in 4.31s
 + cpython-3.13.7-macos-aarch64-none
This asks uv to install the latest available patch release in the 3.13 minor series (Python’s versioning follows major.minor.patch; patch releases are typically bug and security fixes, and are the level of granularity you can usually treat as interchangeable within a project).
Check which Python versions uv can now see on your machine:
uv python list --only-installed
cpython-3.13.7-macos-aarch64-none    /Users/you/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13.7-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.13
Find the exact executable uv would use if you asked for “3.13”:
uv python find 3.13
/Users/you/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13.7-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.13
You can test this interpreter directly, without touching or relying on whatever your computer’s global python command happens to point to:
uv run --python 3.13 python --version
Python 3.13.7

A first check that “your” Python works
Now is a good moment to convince yourself this interpreter runs code, before we build anything more elaborate on top of it:
uv run --python 3.13 python -c "print('Hello from', __import__('sys').version)"
Hello from 3.13.7 (main, ...) [Clang ...]






Tip



uv can also download a missing Python version automatically the first time a project requires it — you do not strictly have to run uv python install yourself in normal use. We are doing it explicitly in this workshop so the installation step is visible and easy to reason about, rather than happening invisibly the first time you create a project.

title: What are the files in the project folder?
text:
After the steps on the previous page, the project folder looks approximately like this:
python-local-demo/
├── .python-version
├── .venv/
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
If you go on to add notebooks, scripts, data documentation, or a README, the project will grow more files and folders around this core. Each of the four items above plays a distinct, non-overlapping role.






Version-control principle



Commit pyproject.toml and uv.lock to Git, alongside your code.
Do not commit .venv/. It is large, platform-specific, generated state, and can always be recreated from the two files above.



pyproject.toml
This is the project’s main, human-edited configuration file. It follows a standard format shared across the modern Python packaging ecosystem (not something specific to uv), which is part of why tools like Poetry and PDM can also read it. A simplified version looks like:
[project]
name = "python-local-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = [
    "jupyterlab",
    "matplotlib",
    "pandas",
]
It records your project’s declared, direct dependencies and its Python compatibility requirement. Note what is absent: no transitive dependencies, and no exact pinned versions — those are deliberately kept in a separate file, described next. You normally edit this list using commands, rather than by hand:
uv add seaborn
uv remove matplotlib


uv.lock
This is the lockfile — the resolved counterpart to the declared list above. It records the complete dependency graph, every transitive dependency, the exact version of each, and a cryptographic hash of the file that was downloaded for each one (so that a future install can verify it received exactly the same bytes, not merely “a” version matching the same version number).
This is what allows uv to reconstruct a bit-for-bit consistent environment later, on a different machine. Do not edit it by hand — treat it as a build artefact that uv maintains for you.
To explicitly (re)create the lockfile from the current pyproject.toml, without touching the installed environment:
uv lock
To create or update the local environment from the current project files (this is what most day-to-day use needs):
uv sync


.python-version
A one-line file recording which Python version this project prefers, for example:
3.13
Change the pin with:
uv python pin 3.13
For particularly strict reproducibility you can pin a full patch version (for example 3.13.7 rather than 3.13), at the cost of having to update that pin deliberately whenever you want a newer patch release.


.venv/
The project’s actual virtual environment: a self-contained folder holding a Python interpreter dedicated to this project, every package installed for it, and any command-line tools those packages provide (such as jupyter).
Treat .venv/ as disposable, generated local state — never something to back up, share, or edit directly. If it is deleted, or corrupted, or you simply want a clean slate, rebuild it from the two files above:
uv sync






What should go into Git?



Usually commit:
pyproject.toml
uv.lock
.python-version
your code
your notebooks
README.md
Usually do not commit:
.venv/
__pycache__/
large generated outputs
secrets or credentials

title: Introduction
text:
Welcome to Installing Python Locally with uv, a short session on setting up a reproducible Python environment for research and teaching.
Almost every computational research project eventually runs into the same problem: code that worked perfectly on one machine fails, produces different numbers, or simply refuses to run on another. Usually the code has not changed — the environment it depends on has.
This short session will explore how to set up a reproducible Python environment for research and teaching. By the end of it you will have installed a modern Python package and project manager, uv, used it to install an isolated Python interpreter, and built a small project whose computational environment can be reconstructed exactly — by you, by a collaborator, or by a peer reviewer — at any point in the future.

Intended learning outcomes
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

explain why recording software versions matters for reproducible research;
install uv and use it to install a specific version of Python;
create a small Python project and identify the files uv uses to describe it;
add and remove Python packages from a project;
run Python or JupyterLab inside the correct project environment.



Software and access required
You will need:

a laptop on which you have permission to install software (if you are on a managed university or company machine and are unsure, ask your local IT support);
a terminal application (PowerShell or Command Prompt on Windows; Terminal on macOS; any terminal emulator on Linux);
an internet connection, to download the uv installer, a Python interpreter, and a small number of packages.

No prior installation of Python is required — part of the point of this session is that uv can provide one for you, without relying on whatever may or may not already be on your computer.


About this course
These course materials have been designed and developed by Pau Erola, PhD (Jean Golding Institute, University of Bristol).
We used the enhancement of AI in alignment with our institutional guidance:

Claude (Sonnet 5) – Writing assistance, expansion of content, and generation of code examples

For queries related to this course please contact jgi-training@bristol.ac.uk.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
uv is not recognised / command not found
First close the terminal completely and open a new one (this reloads your shell’s PATH), then try again:
uv --version
If it still fails, return to the official uv installation instructions and check the alternative installation method listed for your operating system.
On managed university or company computers, software installation or outbound network access may be restricted by policy. Ask your local IT or support team if necessary — this is a legitimate machine restriction, not a step you have done incorrectly.


python --version shows a different version than expected
This can be completely normal if several Python installations are present on your machine — see Multiple Python versions for why.
Inside a project, prefer asking the project directly rather than the bare command:
uv run python --version
To see exactly which executable file is being used:
uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
If that path is not inside your project’s .venv/ folder, something is running outside the project environment — check you are in the correct project directory.


PowerShell will not activate .venv
You do not need to activate the environment at all. Use uv run instead:
uv run python
or:
uv run jupyter lab
This sidesteps PowerShell’s script-execution policy entirely, since no activation script needs to run.


I accidentally deleted .venv/
That is fine — this is exactly the situation uv.lock and pyproject.toml exist for. Recreate the environment from the project files:
uv sync
Then confirm it worked:
uv run python --version


A collaborator has cloned my project
If they have uv installed, they only need to enter the project folder and run:
uv sync
then:
uv run python
uv uses the project’s pyproject.toml and uv.lock to reconstruct a matching environment — they do not need to know, or guess, which packages your project needs.


I want another package
Add it to the project (this updates pyproject.toml, resolves it, updates uv.lock, and installs it, all in one step):
uv add PACKAGE_NAME
For example:
uv add seaborn
Remove one the same way:
uv remove PACKAGE_NAME


uv add or uv sync seems to hang, or fails partway through resolving
This is most often a network issue (a slow or restricted connection to PyPI) rather than a problem with uv or your project. Try again on a different network if one is available, and check with IT support whether outbound access to pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org is permitted on a managed machine.

title: Create a project
text:
A project is simply a folder that has been given a small set of files describing its Python version and dependencies. Creating one gives the environment a permanent home, and gives you files that record its configuration, rather than that configuration existing only in your memory of which commands you happened to type.
Create a folder and move into it:

Windows PowerShellmacOS / Linux


mkdir python-local-demo
cd python-local-demo


mkdir python-local-demo
cd python-local-demo



Now initialise a minimal project using Python 3.13:
uv init --bare --python 3.13 --pin-python
Initialized project `python-local-demo`
Each flag does something specific:

--bare keeps the generated project deliberately minimal — no example script, no README template — which is useful for a short beginner session where we want to look at exactly what got created and understand every line.
--python 3.13 tells uv which Python version to record as this project’s requirement in pyproject.toml.
--pin-python additionally writes a .python-version file, so that any future uv command run inside this folder has an explicit, unambiguous default Python version, even without typing --python again.







Note



If you see instructions elsewhere that use only uv init --bare without pinning a Python version, those are equally valid — uv will simply use whichever compatible Python it finds or installs by default. We are being explicit here because this session’s subject is precisely how to make that choice deliberate and recorded, rather than implicit.



Add some packages
An empty project is not very useful on its own. Add a small set of commonly used research packages:
uv add jupyterlab pandas matplotlib
Resolved 87 packages in 612ms
Prepared 87 packages in 3.94s
Installed 87 packages in 1.21s
 + jupyterlab==4.3.1
 + pandas==2.2.3
 + matplotlib==3.9.2
 ...
A single command has quietly done several things:

updated the project’s declared dependencies in pyproject.toml;
resolved a mutually compatible set of versions for those packages and every package they depend on;
written (or updated) uv.lock with the exact resolution;
created the project’s .venv/ environment, if it did not already exist;
installed every required package — direct and transitive — into that environment.



A first real test
Run Python inside the project’s environment, and check the version:
uv run python --version
Python 3.13.7
Then use a package you just installed, to check it was actually wired up correctly:
uv run python -c "import pandas; print('pandas', pandas.__version__)"
pandas 2.2.3
If that prints a version number rather than an error, your project environment is working end-to-end: the right interpreter, running with the right package installed, resolved and recorded by uv.

title: What are we actually installing?
text:
The instruction “install Python” is deceptively simple. In practice, it bundles together at least four distinct concerns, and most of the confusion people encounter with Python setup comes from not separating them.

An interpreter. The Python interpreter is the program that reads your .py files and executes them. There is no single “Python” — there are numbered versions (3.11, 3.12, 3.13, …) that differ in language features, performance, and package compatibility, and a research group may deliberately need more than one.
Packages. Almost no non-trivial analysis is written from scratch. Libraries such as pandas (tabular data), numpy (numerical arrays), matplotlib (plotting), or jupyterlab (interactive notebooks) provide functionality that would otherwise take months to reimplement. A typical research project depends, directly or indirectly, on tens to hundreds of such packages.
A project environment. Different projects usually need different combinations of packages, and sometimes incompatible versions of the same package. An environment is an isolated location on disk containing exactly the interpreter and packages one project needs, so that installing something for project B cannot silently change what project A sees.
A tool that manages all of the above. Something has to fetch interpreters, resolve which package versions are mutually compatible, install them, and keep a record of what was installed. In this session, that tool is uv.

A bare Python interpreter is sufficient to run a short script, but it is not sufficient for research software: as soon as a second package, a second project, or a second collaborator is involved, you need a systematic way to keep track of what each project requires.

Why not just install everything once, globally?
It is tempting to install Python once and pip install every package you ever need into that single installation. This is what most people do the first time they use Python, and for a single short-lived script it is harmless. It becomes a liability as soon as:

two projects need different, incompatible versions of the same package;
you want to know, months later, exactly which package versions a given piece of analysis used;
you want a collaborator, a peer reviewer, or a continuous-integration server to run your code with the same result you got;
you want to remove a project without worrying about breaking something else that quietly depended on one of its packages.

None of these are hypothetical — package updates that change results, remove functions, or drop support for an old Python version happen routinely in the scientific Python ecosystem. Treating environments as disposable, per-project, and reconstructable from a small number of text files avoids all of the above by construction, rather than by discipline.

title: Hands-on installation
text:
Install Python and build a small, reproducible test project on your own computer. Work through the checklist below in order. If you get stuck, ask for help.

Step 1 — Install uv

WindowsmacOS / Linux


powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"


curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh



Close and reopen your terminal if requested, then check:
uv --version


Step 2 — Install Python
uv python install 3.13
Check it is there:
uv python list --only-installed


Step 3 — Create a project
mkdir python-local-demo
cd python-local-demo
uv init --bare --python 3.13 --pin-python


Step 4 — Add packages
uv add jupyterlab pandas matplotlib


Step 5 — Verify the environment with a small script
Rather than only checking version numbers, create a tiny script that exercises the interpreter and every package you just installed. Save the following as check_setup.py inside python-local-demo/ (use any text editor, or your terminal):
"""Verify that the project environment is set up correctly."""
import sys
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib

print("Python executable:", sys.executable)
print("Python version:   ", sys.version.split()[0])
print("pandas version:   ", pd.__version__)
print("matplotlib version:", matplotlib.__version__)

# A tiny bit of real work, so we are testing behaviour, not just imports
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": range(5), "y": [v * v for v in range(5)]})
print("\nA small DataFrame:")
print(df)
print("\nSum of y:", df["y"].sum())
Run it inside the project environment:
uv run python check_setup.py
Python executable: /Users/you/python-local-demo/.venv/bin/python
Python version:    3.13.7
pandas version:    2.2.3
matplotlib version: 3.9.2

A small DataFrame:
   x   y
0  0   0
1  1   1
2  2   4
3  3   9
4  4  16

Sum of y: 30
If this runs without an error and the Python executable path points inside your project folder’s .venv/, your environment is correctly set up end to end.
Optional — inspect the resolved dependency graph:
uv tree


Step 6 — Start JupyterLab
uv run jupyter lab
A browser window should open automatically. If it does not, look in the terminal output for a local URL beginning with something like:
http://localhost:8888/lab?token=...
and copy that into your browser manually.
Inside JupyterLab, open a new notebook and run the same checks interactively, cell by cell:
import sys
print(sys.executable)
import pandas as pd
pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
To stop JupyterLab, return to the terminal and press Ctrl+C.


Step 7 — Reproducibility check
Look inside your project folder. Can you identify these?
.python-version
pyproject.toml
uv.lock
.venv/
check_setup.py
Explain to the person next to you, or to yourself:

Which files would you commit to Git?
Which directory would you not commit?
Which file records the direct, declared dependencies?
Which file records the resolved, exact dependency versions?
Which command runs Python inside the project’s own environment?







Answers






Commit .python-version, pyproject.toml, uv.lock, check_setup.py, and any other research code or notebooks.
Do not commit .venv/.
pyproject.toml records the project’s declared dependencies.
uv.lock records the resolved dependency graph.
uv run python (or uv run followed by any other command) runs it inside the project environment.






If you finish early

Add another package, for example uv add seaborn, and inspect how pyproject.toml and uv.lock both change.
Run uv tree and try to find a package that is a shared transitive dependency of two of your direct dependencies.
Delete .venv/ entirely and rebuild it with uv sync — confirm check_setup.py still works afterwards.
Compare the output of python --version (your system’s global command) with uv run python --version (the project’s command) — are they the same on your machine?
Install a second Python minor version (for example uv python install 3.12) and inspect uv python list --only-installed.

title: What if I have multiple versions of Python installed?
text:
Having several Python versions installed at once is normal, not a sign of a broken setup. On a typical research machine you might find:

a version supplied by the operating system (used by some system tools — do not remove it);
a version installed from python.org;
a version installed via Homebrew, apt, or another OS-level package manager;
one or more versions installed by uv itself;
separate interpreters living inside individual projects’ .venv/ folders.

These can coexist without conflict because each lives in its own location on disk. Confusion arises not from their coexistence, but from not knowing which one a given command is about to use.

Why this becomes confusing
When you type a bare command such as:
python
your shell searches the directories listed in its PATH environment variable, in order, and runs the first matching executable it finds. That is not necessarily the version you expect, and it can silently differ between two terminal windows, two machines, or before and after installing new software.
You may also encounter several differently-named commands on the same system:
python
python3
python3.12
python3.13
which can point to entirely different interpreters, with different packages installed for each.


Useful diagnostic commands
Rather than guessing, ask directly. See every Python version uv currently knows about:
uv python list --only-installed
Find the executable path for a specific version:
uv python find 3.13
See which version this project is actually using:
uv run python --version
See the interpreter’s exact path from inside Python itself — the most unambiguous check available:
uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
/Users/you/repos/python-local-demo/.venv/bin/python
You can also inspect what your shell itself would find, independently of uv:

WindowsmacOS / Linux


where python
where python3


which -a python
which -a python3





How does uv decide which interpreter to use?
Inside a project, uv consults, in order of specificity: an explicit --python flag on the command line, the project’s .python-version file, the requires-python field in pyproject.toml, and finally the project’s existing .venv/ if one is already built. For example, to bypass a project’s own pin and test explicitly against a different version:
uv run --python 3.13 python --version






Warning



Do not remove or overwrite an operating-system-provided Python just because another version is available. Some OS tools may depend on it internally. Project environments exist precisely so you never need to touch that installation.




Changing a project’s Python version
Minor version changes (for example 3.12 to 3.13) can affect which package versions are compatible, so this is a deliberate environment change, not a cosmetic one. Update the pin:
uv python pin 3.13
then bring the environment back in line with the project files:
uv sync
The recurring theme across this page is: .venv/ is disposable, rebuildable state. The information that actually matters for reproducing your work lives in pyproject.toml and uv.lock — always prefer asking the project which interpreter it is using, over guessing from a bare, global command.
